passage: Our final-year project presentation was the first time I tried it for real. Samir went before me and rushed, his voice climbing higher with every slide. When my name was called, I felt the same thing starting: shoulders creeping up, breath stuck high. So I stood at the front, looked at my first slide, and let one long breath out through my nose. I let my shoulders drop. I counted two silent beats. Then I began: "Good morning. I'm Francis, and our project is about rainwater in hostels." My voice came out lower than I expected, and steady. Nobody noticed the pause; the professor later called me "very composed". Samir asked how I stayed calm. I told him it was just one breath, taken before anyone was looking.

qa.a: The project was about rainwater in hostels.

qa.q: How did Francis feel when the name was called, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Francis felt nervous; the shoulders crept up and the breath got stuck high.

qa.q: Which steps helped Francis begin steadily?
qa.a: One long exhale through the nose, dropping the shoulders and two silent beats before the first sentence.

qa.q: How might Samir feel hearing that it was just one breath?
qa.a: Samir, who rushed and whose voice climbed, may feel hopeful that the trick is simple enough to learn.

grounding: A student slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence, which steadies voice and thinking without anyone noticing.

passage:
Debate coach's notes, college society. Yogesh Tiwari.
Mahima, second year, opened today's inter-college debate. Last month she rushed her first line and lost her thread. Since then we have practised one thing: reach the podium, breathe out slowly, let the shoulders fall, and pause before the first word.
Today I watched from the back row. She stepped up, placed her notes, and I saw her shoulders lower. There was a pause, barely a second. Then her first sentence came out clear and unhurried. I doubt anyone else in the hall noticed a thing; they simply heard a confident speaker. She kept her thread through all four minutes, even when heckled.
Next step: I'll ask her to lead a short breathing warm-up for the first-years before the next round.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh watch from?
qa.a: Yogesh watched from the back row.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt stepping up, given what happened last month?
qa.a: Mahima was probably nervous, remembering how she rushed her first line and lost her thread, but she felt prepared.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh plan to have Mahima lead a breathing warm-up?
qa.a: Mahima has shown the routine works, and teaching it lets first-years learn the same quiet steadying before they speak.

qa.q: How did the audience see Mahima's start?
qa.a: They simply heard a confident speaker and most likely did not notice the brief pause at all.

grounding: A student slows the breath, lowers the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence, which steadies the voice without anyone noticing.

passage:
Friday, 10 pm
Moot court round today. I had the opening submission. When the judge nodded at me, my heart was racing and my shoulders were practically touching my ears. Before, I'd have launched straight in and gabbled. Today I did what I'd practised in the washroom mirror: one long breath out, shoulders down, a second of silence before speaking. It felt like forever, but Pallavi said later it looked like I was simply gathering my notes. My first sentence came out steady, and my thinking stayed clear even when the judge interrupted. Nobody noticed the breath. That's the point. I'm doing it again next round.
Mohit

qa.a: In the washroom mirror.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when the judge nodded?
qa.a: Mohit felt nervous, heart racing and shoulders tense.

qa.q: What three steps did Mohit use before speaking?
qa.a: One long breath out, dropping the shoulders and a second of silence before the first sentence.

qa.q: How did the pause look to Pallavi?
qa.a: To Pallavi it looked as if Mohit was simply gathering notes, not calming nerves.

passage: The panchayat hall in the village near Dharwad was packed with farmers. Chinmay, a third-year agriculture student, had to explain the soil test results he and his classmate Hafsa had collected. As the sarpanch waved him forward, his shoulders crept up and his throat felt tight. He looked down at the chart, breathed out slowly through his mouth, let his shoulders fall and waited one second before speaking. 'Namaskara. We tested the soil from twelve fields.' His voice came out steadier than he expected. When an old farmer questioned the results, Chinmay took another quiet breath before answering, and his thinking stayed clear. Afterwards Hafsa said, 'You looked so calm.' He laughed. 'Inside, not so much. But the breath helps.'

qa.q: How many fields did Chinmay and Hafsa test?
qa.a: Twelve fields.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling as the sarpanch waved him forward?
qa.a: He was nervous, with his shoulders creeping up and his throat tight.

qa.q: Which choice helped when the old farmer questioned the results?
qa.a: Taking another quiet breath before answering kept Chinmay's thinking clear instead of rushed.

qa.q: How did Hafsa see Chinmay during the talk?
qa.a: Hafsa thought he looked calm, because his steady breathing did its work quietly, without anyone noticing.

passage: In the seminar room at the university in Buenos Aires, Mateo was next to present his thesis proposal. Selin, beside him, fidgeted with her notes and whispered how nervous she was. Mateo felt his own heart thumping. He stood, walked to the front and, before saying a word, let out a long, slow breath through his mouth. He dropped his shoulders, looked at the first slide and paused for a moment. Nobody noticed; to them he was just getting ready. His first sentence came out steady, and his voice stayed level even when the professor interrupted with a question. Afterwards Selin asked how he stayed so calm. 'One long breath out,' he said. 'Want to try it before yours?'

qa.q: What did Mateo do before saying a word?
qa.a: Let out a long, slow breath through his mouth.

qa.q: How was Mateo feeling as he stood up?
qa.a: He felt nervous, with his heart thumping.

qa.q: Why did Mateo's small routine work?
qa.a: The slow exhale and dropped shoulders steadied his voice and thinking, quietly, without anyone noticing.

qa.q: How might Selin feel when Mateo offers to share the trick?
qa.a: Selin probably feels relieved and grateful, hoping it will steady her own nerves.

grounding: A student slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before presenting, steadying voice and thinking unnoticed.
